#1197. New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers tagged dozens of proteins that can cross the blood-brain barrier and are important for brain health.Credit: K. H. Fung/SPL

For decades, scientists thought of the blood–brain barrier as an impenetrable layer. Over time that view has changed, as researchers realized the barrier was more permeable than first thought. Now, a team have catalogued almost 100 proteins that can pass through it to maintain brain health1.

The team also found that the transport of some of these crucial proteins breaks down in mice with brain diseases that mimic early-stage Alzheimer’s disease.

“The paradigm in the field has been that the blood–brain barrier is normally impermeable and then becomes leaky as a result of Alzheimer’s disease,” says study co-author Andrew Yang, a neuroscientist at Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease in San Francisco, California. Instead, his team’s work suggests that the blood–brain barrier actively imports proteins that the brain needs to function and the loss of these proteins drives the dysfunction seen early in the disease, he adds.

Yang and his colleagues developed a technique to label a large array of proteins in the blood and track those that can enter the brain. Of the 861 proteins they mapped, 92 crossed the blood–brain barrier into the brain. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver.

The team focused on apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), which has been linked to potential protective effects against Alzheimer’s disease2. Once inside the brain, APOA1 stimulates brain cells called astrocytes to release cholesterol, which is important for maintaining the synapses through which neurons communicate. But how the protein crossed the blood–brain barrier has been unclear until now, says Yang.

His team found that two receptors for APOA1 — SR-B1 and ABCA1 — are present on the blood–brain barrier as well as astrocytes. This suggests how the protein moves from the blood–brain barrier to the specific brain cells that need them, the authors say.

When Yang’s team blocked the ABCA1 receptor in laboratory-grown astrocytes, the protein no longer had the same cholesterol-regulating effects.

Scientists have long known that the blood–brain barrier breaks down as Alzheimer’s advances, letting harmful molecules leak into the brain. Yang’s team found that a different problem emerges first.

Using their labelling technique in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease, the researchers found that the blood–brain barrier stopped importing protective proteins such as APOA1 into the brain before the barrier began to break down. This disruption to the protein transport was accompanied by a loss of neuronal connections, behavioural changes and other early hallmarks of the disease.

Yang and the team wondered whether increasing the supply of APOA1 in the blood might help to counter some of the damage caused by Alzheimer’s disease. To find out, the team engineered mice with Alzheimer’s to produce extra APOA1 in the liver. When more APOA1 crossed the blood–brain barrier and entered the brain, the mice showed fewer Alzheimer’s-disease-related markers. For example, they had reduced fat build-up in astrocytes and lower levels of inflammatory molecules.

#1196. OLIVER HOLT: Man United fans' anti-Glazer walkout flopped because owners don't care - but it's not impossible to oust them. Here's what they should do instead

Published: 09:02 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 12:54 EST, 9 November 2026

The only chance I ever got at holding one of the Glazer family to account in person for what they were doing to Manchester United came in Tampa, Florida, in 2009, a few days before the Super Bowl between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Arizona Cardinals. As interrogations go, mine was rather feeble.

I was there for the game but I noticed that, as part of the week’s build-up to it, Bryan Glazer was speaking at an NFL Kids Day. The event was held outdoors, in the grounds of the Raymond James Stadium and it was open to the media so I went along and listened to Bryan speak.

As he left, I wandered over to speak to him. Everything was relaxed until I introduced myself as an English sports journalist and asked him about his family’s stewardship of United. Glazer’s smile stiffened and then it disappeared.

He didn’t say a single word. He did not break his stride. He glanced meaningfully at a security guy, who was part of his entourage, and the security guy stepped across me and blocked my path. Glazer kept walking, climbed on to a golf buggy and was driven away.

Seventeen years down the line and few have got more out of the Glazers than that stiffened smile – although Avram Glazer did tell an audience of financiers at Deutsche Bank’s inaugural Sports Investment Conference in London recently that sports teams at United’s level are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. He would say that.

That went down well among United supporters, obviously, and as United languish in the Premier League’s bottom three, one point off the foot of the table, anger against the Glazer ownership, which has cost the club more than £1billion in debt interest payments and shareholder dividends, is rising to a crescendo again.

Matheus Cunha (left) and Bruno Fernandes come to terms with another disappointing Manchester United performance after the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday

The United fans made clear what they think of their owners at Old Trafford

Anger against the Glazers has been fuelled by disenchantment with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the minority owner, whose involvement in the football operation has deepened and widened the disillusionment of the fanbase with the people who are fiddling while United burns in decline. It is 40 years since United were in the relegation zone after more than nine games.

‘We Don’t Want A New Stadium, We Want New Owners,’ a banner in the Stretford End read. The idea of getting rid of the Glazers and Ratcliffe has become a panacea for United supporters. It is seen as the key to the club’s recovery, the key to everything, but the struggle to dislodge them faces huge obstacles.

The protests are redoubling. Old Trafford was awash with green and gold, the colours of tradition and disaffection at the club, for the chaotic draw against Aston Villa on Sunday afternoon and the stadium echoed to deafening chants calling for the Glazers to get out of United. Battalions of green and gold balloons took to the air before kick-off.

The problem is that the Glazers do not care. They run the club by remote control from Florida. They are detached. They always have been. I have watched protest marches before and seen supporters gathering at the start, outside the Tollgate pub a mile or so from the ground, in impressive numbers. They have achieved little.

It is not impossible for fans to oust or defy owners. The power of supporters was at its most inspiring when it faced down the plans of Manchester City, Chelsea, Spurs, United, Arsenal and Liverpool to join a breakaway European Super League in 2021.

In Germany, some years ago, when plans were revealed to stage Monday night games, there was widespread outrage at the idea of supporters having to travel to games after work. Dissent and disobedience followed.

Tennis balls were thrown on to pitches during games, a chorus of vuvuzelas filled the air, remote-controlled cars sped on to the playing surface. Monday night games were dropped.

Liverpool removed co-owners Tom Hicks and George Gillett in October 2010 through a combination of an independent board, a High Court legal battle, and pressure from the Royal Bank of Scotland, all underpinned by huge supporter demonstrations and campaigns against the US owners.

I once confronted Bryan Glazer over his family’s stewardship of United. His smile stiffened and then disappeared

Supporters have had enough - but how far are they willing to go to drive the Glazers out?

And on a smaller, but no less heroic, scale, Blackpool supporters staged a four-year boycott of their team’s matches, starting in 2015, that saw the average attendance at Bloomfield Road drop from 10,000 to 2,500 and was critical in the removal from the club of the much-loathed owners, the Oyston Family.

That Blackpool protest movement is the subject of a soon-to-be-aired documentary on Sky called Don’t F*** With Fans. One of the main lessons that the programme preaches is the need for unity in a fanbase if the protests are to have any chance of succeeding.

Achieving that unity has already been made harder at clubs like United because of the way the loyal supporter base is being diluted by the war on traditional season-ticket holders and the move towards attracting more day-trippers and tourists, who will spend more for the price of admission and more at the club superstore.

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it. The popular YouTuber SaeedTV was one of them.

‘I did my bit,’ he posted on X as he stood outside the stadium almost alone. ‘Unfortunately fans don’t care enough. Glazers OUT INEOS OUT.’

Part of the problem the call for boycotts faces is that tourists don’t do protest. They have paid too much for their seat to walk out midway through the first half.

Many of the calls for a mass walkout also come from fans on social media, who are not match-going supporters. Fans who do go to the games are, understandably, reluctant to walk out when they have paid for their seats. They also know that if they were to give up their season tickets, the club would be delighted.

Some match-going fans started a tongue-in-cheek campaign aimed at armchair fans who have been trying to preach to them how best to get the Glazers out. ‘Turn off your television sets after 21 minutes,’ was the gist of it.

But the fact remains that unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United. History says a form of co-ordinated, well-orchestrated, mass-participation peaceful disobedience is the only way.

Unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it

It has to be something that affects the spectacle and, more specifically, the optics for television viewers. And it has to be something that affects them consistently.

Many Premier League clubs don’t care about match-going fans anymore but if the television product is affected, if the broadcasters become concerned, if sponsors start to think that they might actually be damaged by association with the disaffection at Manchester United, then maybe at least a little pressure would be brought to bear on an ownership group.

The odds are stacked more and more heavily against supporters who wish to effect change. But the opposition to the European Super League showed it could be done. The Blackpool fan boycott showed it could be done. Liverpool supporters’ demonstrations against Hicks and Gillett showed it could be done.

It is a question of whether the will exists. Of whether the unity exists. And of whether there are simply too many of the new breed of fan who would rather take selfies and queue for merchandise than turn the club back into an institution that cares more for trophies than revenue.

#1184. Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

A study suggests that people are being misdiagnosed as having obesity with a metric known as the body mass index (BMI).Credit: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty

Clinicians have debated for years whether body mass index (BMI) — a metric derived from a person’s height and weight — is the best way to define and diagnose obesity. Now, an approach that measures waist circumference and focuses more closely on excess body fat has proved to be better than BMI at predicting a person’s risk of death.

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

An analysis of data collected from more than 800,000 individuals found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The study was published today in Nature1.

Physicians know that BMI — calculated by dividing a person’s weight by the square of their height — doesn’t accurately reflect body composition. For example, a muscular person might have an elevated BMI but have little body fat. The latest study “reinforces that BMI is not a good measure of obesity at the individual level and is not good in terms of predicting who is going to develop cardiometabolic disease in the long term”, says Cátia Martins, an obesity researcher at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

But given how simple it is to calculate BMI, it remains the most widely used tool to classify obesity.

A person is usually diagnosed with obesity if they have a BMI of 30 or higher. The approach presented in the study — called the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, or CAD-obesity — goes beyond BMI, combining it with measures, such as waist circumference, that are linked to excess body fat. Physicians know that when fat tissue is preferentially stored in the abdominal area, it is associated with more negative health consequences than when it’s stored elsewhere, Martins says.

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Under the CAD-obesity system2, first proposed last year, people with obesity who also have at least one of 18 specific health problems — including heart failure and sleep apnoea — are classified as having ‘clinical obesity’. This indicates that excess fat is harming their organs and tissues. Those with obesity but none of these health problems are classified as having ‘preclinical obesity’, in which a person has excess fat but their organs are functioning normally.

“We did not know until now whether or not this new framework had implications in the real world and a prognostic value,” says Francesco Rubino, a weight-loss surgeon at King’s College London who led the effort to create the system and is a co-author of the Nature paper.

But Rubino and his colleagues proved the system’s worth by examining medical records from four large groups of people in China, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. They used data from three of those cohorts, in which more than 50,000 deaths occurred over up to 15 years, to determine whether BMI or the CAD-obesity system was a better indicator of elevated mortality risk.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5

#1180. Why Chelsea aren't European contenders, Tottenham aren't 'back'... and Brighton and Bournemouth are in a title race: What you should believe and what's just a mirage after 10 Premier League games - and the proof behind it

Published: 12:18 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 03:11 EST, 10 November 2026

We are ten games into the Premier League season and another international break provides the ideal opportunity to take stock on what has been a bewildering start to another campaign.

Michael Carrick heads off for a couple of weeks with Manchester United still in the bottom three. Brighton perch second in the Premier League behind Arsenal, who are threatening to run away with it. Tottenham are only a point outside the top half, which is enough on its own to make you squint and rub your eyes. That can’t be right.

We are more than a quarter of the way through now, enough time for patterns to emerge and directions of travel to settle but also not long enough for us to be entirely sure who’s still benefitting from an early hot streak or suffering from unfair misfortune.

Who is where they belong? What can we believe? Daily Mail Sport digs into the numbers to figure out what’s real and what is fake about this Premier League season so far...

REAL: Defences CAN win you titles, just ask Arsenal

Sir Alex Ferguson was wrong, of course, when he declared that ‘attack wins you games, defence wins you titles’. Over the 31 completed 20-team Premier League seasons, fewer than half of them were won by the team that conceded the fewest goals. More than two thirds of them, however, were won by the side that scored the most.

Sometimes, as was often the case during the Pep Guardiola era, teams can be the best at both. Of the 15 times since 1995-96 that the best defence triumphed, they were also the most prolific attack on nine occasions.

Arsenal's goals, xG, shots and shots on target are all at their lowest per game since Mikel Arteta’s first season in charge. But thanks to their defence, they are five points clear at the top

Arsenal, however, are certainly not that. Their title win last season was only the sixth time in the previous 30 years that the best defence alone was crowned champions. They are doing it again this season, five points clear and proving that the best defence can still win you a title on its own.

And it’s a good job, too, because while their defence is as rock-solid as ever, their attack is getting worse. Last season, the Gunners ranked second for goals but fourth for expected goals (xG) and shots. This term, they are sixth for goals, fifth for xG and 10th for shots.

Their goals, xG, shots and shots on target are all at their lowest per game since Arteta’s first season in charge. Their win over Hull was their fourth 1-0 victory of the campaign. Not that Arteta will care. His defence means they still have the best xG difference in the division and it’s going to win him another league title.

That euphoric 3-1 victory over Manchester City was coming. There had been a fair amount of noise building around Oliver Glasner’s start to life on the Trent as Nottingham Forest went into the weekend second from bottom in the Premier League.

One defeat in nine. Was it Glasner’s new system taking time to bed in like it did at Crystal Palace? How quickly would ‘Mr Marinakis’ lose his patience this time around and fire another head coach?

This time last year, Forest were already on to their third manager of the season. Patience, for once, will reap its rewards. Forest didn’t deserve to be 19th. They have the fifth-best expected goal difference in the division. When you dig into the numbers, Forest have the best defence of any team not named Arsenal.

Fewest shots faced, second-fewest shots on target faced after the Gunners, second lowest xG conceded after, yep, Arsenal. They have made the fewest errors leading to shots all season with just two. Bournemouth are next on five.

Their problem is they, somehow, have not been able to score. Only Sunderland – another side doing worse than their expected numbers would suggest – have underperformed their xG in front of goal more than Forest. I was at Crystal Palace for Glasner’s return to Selhurst Park and, quite simply, Forest should have been 4-0 up by half-time.

They have the lowest shot conversion rate of any side in the league at just 5.5 per cent. That’s unsustainably low. Only one team since 2014-15 has maintained one as low as that across an entire season and that was Huddersfield in 2018-19, when they finished bottom with 16 points. Forest are nowhere near that bad.

Their need for a striker has long been obvious and if Liam Delap’s brace against City can spark some confidence and form, they might have the striker they need to start climbing up the table and, who knows, into European contention.

Nottingham Forest will hope Liam Delap's brilliant brace against Manchester City is the start of them getting past their woes in front of goal

Listen to Jamie O’Hara on talkSPORT after a run of three wins on the trot, and he might have you believing that Spurs are back.

Along with another defeat, this time to Leeds, to bring Spurs hurtling to earth, their numbers simply are not good enough – and certainly not in attack – to be deemed as such.

They may have attempted the fifth-most shots in the division but in doing so have still put up the fourth-worst xG, as their xG per shot is the worst in the division. In short: they shoot a lot but hardly ever from anywhere dangerous. That 40 per cent of their goals have come from outside the box, the highest in the league, is unsustainable.

They just don’t create enough. Left back Andy Robertson has created the most chances for Spurs this season with 14. Twenty-seven players have created more than him so far, with 15 other clubs boasting at least one star higher than Tottenham’s top man. Sunderland have two above him and Arsenal, Brighton and Manchester United have three.

Tottenham have the worst xG per shot in the league - meaning they rarely get into good positions to score

REAL: Brighton (and maybe Bournemouth) are in a title race

We have got used to seeing these modest but exceptionally run clubs punching above their weight in the Premier League but even the most appreciative of us could not have expected to see at least one of them in a title race.

If, by title race, we mean the team that might get closest to Arsenal. Looking at the underlying numbers, it could even be both of them.

When you look at the expected goal difference of all clubs in the division – those you should have scored from the quality of the chances you create, against those you should have conceded from the quality of the ones you allow your opponents to create – Bournemouth and Brighton sit behind only Arsenal and Man City.

Brighton are the division’s top scorers by a distance, five more than anyone else, but even though they are outperforming their expected numbers (their players can’t keep scoring one in every 10 shots they take from outside the box – looking at you, Diego Gomez) the Seagulls are still putting up the second biggest xG behind City.

Of the 11 players to create more than 20 chances so far, Brighton are the only side to have two names in there in Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. They also, of course, beat Arsenal and City without conceding to either team.

They do need to get tighter at the back if they wish to stay near the top, mind. Brighton should have conceded about seven more goals than they have done. No side has overperformed their defensive data quite so much.

Bournemouth are the ones who should be doing better, which sounds mad for a team that’s just won eight games on the bounce in less than a month in all competitions. The Cherries sit seventh but have the third-best xG, and the third-best xG conceded. That, no matter how you look at it, is a recipe for prolonged success.

Brighton's Diego Gomez can't continue scoring every shot he has from long range... can he?

Bournemouth are the ones who should be doing better, which sounds mad for a team that’s just won eight games on the bounce in less than a month

Speaking of overperforming, few teams are doing quite so well to hide their abundant flaws as Chelsea. Xabi Alonso’s side sit fifth in the Premier League and the Spaniard can be thankful to the football gods for it. They should not be fifth.

Chelsea sit in the bottom half for both xG for and against. Their expected goal difference puts them in 14th, below Fulham, Manchester United and Sunderland.

Only Brighton have scored more goals than they should have done based on their chances but, unlike the Seagulls, Chelsea’s baseline is far more mediocre. Opta’s expected points table has them 12th.

They are also one of only two sides in the division this season not to have had a single goal scored by a substitute.

Chelsea's expected goal difference puts them in 14th, below Fulham, Manchester United and Sunderland

When you lose a manager as influential as Eddie Howe, it’s always going to be a tricky transition. When you sell Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon and struggle to replace them adequately, it’s going to be harder still.

Still, Newcastle should be doing better. They should not be creating better chances than only Hull and Coventry. Their expected goal difference is only better than Coventry, Ipswich and Palace. Opta’s expected table has them just outside the relegation zone.

Only three teams have faced more shots, only three have attempted more shots on target, only five have played fewer passes into the box.

Daily Mail Sport revealed last week that Newcastle’s players are ‘confused’ by new manager Matthias Jaissle’s instructions, playing style and strategy. Jaissle accused his team after the defeat to Everton of not following his instructions or executing the tactics they had worked on in training.

They have to find a way of getting it to click after the international break otherwise they will be fighting out most of their season closer to that dotted line.

It can often be fun for supporters of other clubs around the country to revel in the pain and misery that Manchester United appear intent on inflicting on their own supporters.

Even the carnage and chaos of coming from two goals down against Aston Villa and the shot of joy that can bring was still only enough to leave United 18th in the table.

Do they deserve to be there? With just one win all season, the fewest in the league, you would think so. United have, perhaps, not quite been that bad – but they certainly don’t help themselves.

Everyone talks about them having tons of shots, which they do. They have had the most in the division by a distance, which always keeps the xG totting up, but so many of them come from miles away. United, too often, take the scattergun approach.

Manchester United have been suffering from bad luck at the back - but will it correct itself in time to save them from a relegation battle?

Their xG per shot is the lowest in the division, meaning their shots aren’t from dangerous positions, and their conversion rate is one of the worst, too. When 45 per cent of your attempts on goal come from outside the box, that’s likely to happen. That makes their midtable expected goal difference slightly misleading.

Their main problem is at the back – and that is where they are being consistently punished. It is the opposite story to their attack.

United have faced among the fewest shots in the division but among the most on target. Their xG per shot faced is the highest in the league, and their opponents enjoy a higher conversion rate than against any other team.

That, though, is unlikely to remain sustainable. They are unlikely to keep getting punished quite so harshly. That should be enough to drag them clear – but only just.

It is always worth remembering that you only get a true reading of the Premier League table after ten games so this is a pivotal moment for both Newcastle and Everton as they play their ninth match of the campaign.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. The table is starting to take shape and so are the narratives around every club.

Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

#1173. Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Minimalist biotechnology companies that have just a handful of employees — or even as few as one — are becoming more feasible with the rise of artificial-intelligence tools.Credit: Getty

How many scientists does it take to discover a drug?

The question came to the fore after news that a biotechnology company armed with an artificial-intelligence assistant, two promising drug leads and just one full-time human employee had been acquired by San Francisco-based Anthropic as part of the AI giant’s expansion into biomedical science.

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

In truth, it took many human scientists to develop the molecules that are the mini-company’s star products: two antibodies that are still in the early stages of development and were designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy. The company, Mithril Medicine in Cambridge, Massachusetts, also hired part-time consultants to advise on the project, and paid at least five contract research organizations to conduct experiments. Many more researchers will be needed to carry the drug further, especially if it eventually enters clinical trials. “It takes a village to develop a drug,” says Jeb Keiper, a partner at Third Rock Ventures, a venture-capital firm in Boston, Massachusetts.

But the news sparked a wave of discussions about whether the one-person biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future. “We will see more and more of these small teams that are enabled by AI,” says James Zou, a computer scientist who works on biomedical applications of AI at Stanford University in California. “They will be very powerful for identifying good opportunities and moving quickly.”

Itsy-bitsy biotechs are not a new concept. Entrepreneur Matt Davidson started his first biotech company in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT’s public debut. Davidson kept the roster trim for years, with only two full-time employees until the drug he was developing was ready to enter late-stage clinical testing. The company never had a physical laboratory, Davidson says. All the lab work was contracted out.

His current company, Azora Therapeutics in Los Angeles, California, has a whopping five employees. He uses AI more for summarizing reports than for scientific discovery and says that AI tools have made tiny biotechs more efficient. “We use consultants a little bit less than we used to,” he says.

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Mithril Medicine leaned more heavily on AI than Azora does, and tasked Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude with helping to analyse data and suggesting next steps, as well as taming the piles of e-mails and paperwork that come from working with multiple contract research organizations. “What began as an exercise in staying lean evolved into the thesis for an entirely new operating model, which we now call Pipeline-in-a-Person,” wrote Cody Tranbarger, Mithril’s former chief executive and lone employee, on LinkedIn. (Tranbarger, who has worked for Anthropic since Mithril was absorbed into it, declined to speak to Nature, as did Anthropic.)

#1169. How Michael Carrick's Man United fell apart: Players' bust-up on flight back from Madrid, weakness in training and on touchline - and why dressing-room sources believe divided board 'hung him out to dry'

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 10:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 06:44 EST, 12 November 2026

For the last two days, Michael Carrick has followed his familiar route towards Manchester United’s training base, nudging his black Land Rover past the security barrier at Carrington before 8am, and making his way into work just as he has for much of the last two decades as a player, coach and head coach at the club.

While Carrick's fate has been decided by men in suits in Monaco and Manchester, he has put on his training gear and gone through the motions of coaching whichever players are left during the international break.

It has become increasingly apparent that Carrick was a dead man walking in the two weeks since the United board gave him a stay of execution and bought themselves time after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month.

Having effectively been brought in as a caretaker when United plucked him off the beach in Barbados in mid-January, he left much the same way: merely keeping the seat warm for Mauricio Pochettino in the chaotic days that have led to his sacking.

Sources close to the United dressing room believe Carrick has been ‘hung out to dry’ as United dithered over his future and then began a futile attempt to appoint Pochettino as his replacement in secret.

This is the story of how Carrick's United fell apart. It is the story of how disgruntled players aired their dirty laundry in public and clashed in private. It is the story of how the club's boardroom became the backdrop for an executive power struggle. And it is the story of how the magic touch that saw Carrick land the job permanently just five months ago deserted him...

Michael Carrick is out as Manchester United manager - just ten league games after guiding United to third and being handed a two-year contract

Carrick has had to turn up as normal at Carrington this week even as the world knew he was for the chop. Some dressing-room sources say he has been 'hung out to dry'

Carrick would have seen the writing on the wall when he got up to give an impressive speech at a dinner in the Heritage Suite at Old Trafford on Friday night to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Sir Alex Ferguson’s appointment.

The significance of the occasion was not lost on Carrick. Ferguson was brought in to succeed Ron Atkinson on the same date in November 1986 with United one place above the relegation zone. Having boxed himself into an identical corner, Carrick too was on borrowed time.

Two days later, he stood helplessly on the touchline at Old Trafford as United played out a ridiculous 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Twice his team fought back from two goals down, but it was the final proof for United bosses that change was unavoidable.

The biggest club in English football having to endure the humiliation of at least two weeks in the relegation zone was too much for them to stomach.

His body language after the Bournemouth game when a tearful and crestfallen Carrick offered what looked like a farewell wave to the Stretford End – four days after he approached fans in Como to apologise for an equally painful 4-1 Champions League surrender – suggested he was already done.

The 45-year-old limped on to another defeat at Chelsea, then presided over a barmy 3-2 comeback win over Roma and the bonkers draw with Villa. A consummate and composed midfielder for United, Carrick of all people knew this wasn’t the way football should be played.

All the while, he spoke like a man who could turn things around. They always do. But the performances and results told a different story.

His critics would argue that someone whose only previous job in management was at Middlesbrough should never have been put in charge of United in the first place.

Others would say the bravest move by the club would have been to thank Carrick for his admirable efforts in securing third place and Champions League qualification last season, and move on in the summer when Pochettino would have been available for free before signing a new contract as US coach with a £7million release clause.

Matheus Cunha's late winner sealed a remarkable comeback win over Roma last week - but it promised to be a false dawn for Carrick

The 45-year-old's body language after an earlier loss to Bournemouth had suggested he was done back then, with Carrick appearing to wave farewell to the Stretford End

Instead, Carrick was rewarded with a two-year deal in May and the wheels fell off in spectacular fashion. Rather like his friend and former team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, the honeymoon period gave way to something altogether less appealing.

At least Solskjaer stuck around for three more years. Having beaten the Norwegian to the job in January, Carrick’s reign lasted less than 10 months.

The similarities between the two men are striking. Ex-players who basked in the glory days under Ferguson and know what it takes to succeed at Old Trafford, but were incapable of lifting the modern-day Manchester United to similar heights.

Having replaced Ruben Amorim and inspired a remarkable turnaround in the second half of last season, Carrick must have thought he had a chance.

His calm demeanour and experience of life in the Old Trafford pressure cooker that had played a part in his appointment was in contrast to the emotional incontinence of Amorim. How strange then that it has given way to such calamity and chaos.

United got off to the worst possible start by losing at newly-promoted Hull City in August. Tigers boss Sergej Jakirovic belittled them by saying his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis might as well have been sipping a cup of tea, and the hits have just kept on coming for Carrick.

Aside from Bournemouth, there were the late equalisers scored by Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Dominic Solanke for Everton and Tottenham, the controversial winner conceded to 10-man Manchester City, crashing out of the Carabao Cup to Brighton after giving up a two-goal lead, and the defeats in Europe by Atletico Madrid and Como after going behind in the opening seconds.

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. The four goals Carrick’s side conceded took it to 15 in his final four games.

United's defence has been leaky all season long, with Ainsley Maitland-Niles' stoppage-time equaliser at Hill Dickinson Stadium among the goals to cost them valuable points

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Aston Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. They let in 15 in his final four games

So why the alarming decline from last season? The United players haven’t looked sharp after a disjointed World Cup summer that involved a more relaxed one-week training camp in Ireland. There have been too many injuries.

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff. Others feel that the switch to a more possession-based 4-2-4 system was asking too much of a group who aren’t suited to it.

There was surprise that a man so invested in the club's academy used so few young players. Harry Amass was left kicking his heels despite the chronic shortage of left backs, JJ Gabriel's shock exit was an unwelcome distraction, and Shea Lacey's re-emergence came too late.

It would be grossly unfair to pin this all on Carrick though. He is just the latest unfortunate to pay the price for the shambles at United which runs from the boardroom to the dressing room.

Amid ongoing uncertainty over his future, there has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell over who to replace him, while sources close to the Glazer family have revealed a growing dissatisfaction at how minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos are running the club.

United failed Carrick in the transfer market last summer with a futile pursuit of his No 1 midfield target Elliot Anderson, and instead delivered Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

Carrick could see trouble on the horizon when he spoke to the media at Carton House in Maynooth during that pre-season camp in early August, but tried not to rock the boat.

It was the day his daughter Louise was getting her A-level results. ‘You know, we would like more, we need to keep pushing for more,’ he said, using the word ‘push’ another nine times.

There has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox (centre) and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell (left) over who to replace Carrick

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff

Carlos Baleba followed but an ankle injury meant that he couldn’t play until October, and the £70m signing then suffered a hamstring injury.

United blundered catastrophically by focusing on midfield and delaying improvements to other areas of the team until next summer. In particular, the decision not to sign cover for Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko backfired spectacularly as both players succumbed to injury.

Lisandro Martinez called out United’s underwhelming recruitment in Madrid by saying he expected more of Wilcox, and he isn’t the only one who feels that way.

Tielemans gave a terse ‘no comment’ when he was asked on camera about his team-mate’s remarks, but it’s understood the two players clashed on the team flight back to Manchester as cracks began to show in an increasingly unhappy camp.

The camaraderie fostered by rounds of golf involving Carrick and the players during the break in Ireland was beginning to fall apart.

It came to a head when captain Bruno Fernandes became the second member of the leadership group to speak out of turn, questioning Carrick’s tactics after the loss to Como.

Having continuously defended his players in the face of criticism from some of his former United team-mates over their lack of effort, Carrick’s spiky response that ‘if you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren’t going to win’ perhaps revealed his true feelings about this group.

He and Fernandes settled their differences in a clear-the-air meeting, but the questions didn’t go away. When he was asked about their relationship again at the end of what proved to be his final pre-match press conference last Friday, Carrick tapped his inquisitor on the shoulder as he left the room at Carrington and said with a smile: ‘Nice try!’

It was typical of Carrick, who often met questions with the knowing grin of a man who couldn’t say what he really thought.

Lisandro Martinez and Youri Tielemans clashed on United's flight back to Manchester following the former's incendiary comments after a loss to Atletico Madrid

One issue has been Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline. ‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source

It got to the point where he was encouraged by the club to be a little more forthcoming in press conferences. There have been some barbed post-match exchanges in TV interviews with Sky Sports and Viaplay this season, and the five-minute monologue before the Bournemouth game was pure theatre.

But on the whole, Carrick’s ability to play a straight bat in front of the cameras was a welcome change for the Old Trafford hierarchy compared to the loose-lipped Amorim – particularly with the Amazon Prime documentary-makers following their every move.

‘He talks a lot but doesn't say much,’ said Roy Keane, never Carrick’s biggest fan, on Sunday. ‘I don't know if that's a tactic, like a politician.’

More of an issue was Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline, which seemed to be reflected in his team at times.

Always dressed in black, a hand placed studiously on his chin, it has contrasted with more animated adversaries such as Unai Emery, Roberto De Zerbi and Diego Simeone in recent weeks.

‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source.

The fans were always behind him though, even the ones who may have accepted some time ago that a change was needed. Support and sympathy were never in short supply for a coach who has been let down by the men in the directors’ box and the players on the pitch.

That much has been abundantly clear by the abuse meted out to Ratcliffe and Co this season, and the unprecedented scenes when the fans turned on the players after Bournemouth.

Carrick looks set to be replaced by former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino (right)

Carrick has been known to stand alongside them in the past, and it would be no surprise to see him there again in future.

‘Oh, it’s Carrick you know…’ echoed his tribute song from the Stretford End as he disappeared down the tunnel for the last time on Sunday evening.

So another bites the dust. A good man. A United man. The right man for the job? Maybe not, as it turns out. That poisoned chalice now passes to Mauricio Pochettino.

#1163. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

From being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

The difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

On the pitch, United were all over the place. Carrick had dropped Lisandro Martínez after his red card against Chelsea but his replacement Ayden Heaven was at fault for the first goal after getting sucked in and failing to check his shoulder. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

At that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

It has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Feel free to drop us your score predictions in the comments – bragging rights on the line for the winner.

We’ll be bringing you team news, previews from the managers and more ahead of kick-off at 8pm!

#1161. Give biologists the space to be curious, not just better tools

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Edith Heard is the chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London.

As the Francis Crick Institute in London celebrates its tenth anniversary and I look back on my first year as chief executive, I find myself reflecting on both how much has been achieved and how profoundly life science is changing.

As an epigeneticist, I can safely say that history and context matter. When I began my scientific career in the 1980s, experiments were painstaking, time-consuming, expensive and repetitive. Generating a knockout mouse or sequencing a gene could take weeks or months, and required resources that were available at few institutions.

The Selfish Gene, 50 years on — it’s time for an update

The Selfish Gene, 50 years on — it’s time for an update

Biology has since entered an extraordinary era. It is increasingly multidisciplinary, and researchers have an unprecedented range of technologies at their disposal, from single-cell and spatial biology techniques to advanced imaging, genome editing, tissue engineering and computational approaches.

Artificial intelligence is also transforming science. Its ability to bring together complex data sets offers fresh ways to connect the study of biology across scales, from molecules and cells to individual organisms and populations. It is also enabling the democratization of discovery and knowledge. Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold system, for example, has made predictions of millions of protein structures available to researchers worldwide.

Biologists are poised to at last understand the complexity of life: the influence of the environment, ageing and sex, alongside genetics, on the differences between us. Among the questions to which answers are within reach are how the genetic code gives rise to a living organism; how the control and expression of genes varies during development; how tissues communicate and bodily functions depend on one another; and why diseases develop differently in different people and treatments work for some but not others.

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

Reductionism has served biology well, giving us a deep mechanistic understanding of life, health and disease. But many features of living systems cannot be predicted from their individual parts alone. They emerge from interactions between components and depend on the context in which those interactions occur.

Science needs both reductionist and holistic approaches: connecting molecular mechanisms and signalling pathways with inter-organ communication and physiology, while understanding how these systems respond and adapt to environmental challenges. And performing such studies requires research environments that allow scientists to think and work across conventional boundaries.

As director of the Crick, I have seen the incredible value of an environment that is organized around people and scientific questions rather than institutional divisions. Shared infrastructure and specialist teams enable research to cross disciplines and deploy technologies in new ways. Connections between fundamental research, clinical science and industry also help discoveries to move towards real-world applications, swiftly and efficiently.

But even the most sophisticated technologies and research environments are only as powerful as the scientists using them. Creating an environment in which people from diverse backgrounds and with different life experiences are encouraged to perform bold, rigorous science and harness the power of AI will be key to future discoveries. Patterns identified by AI need to be scrutinized by people and validated through experiment.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03669-w

#1159. 'I was one day away from falling into a coma': JAKE O'BRIEN, the Premier League's only diabetic player, on his brush with death, managing his condition in the dressing room - and why he was 'never close' to leaving Everton last summer

Published: 21:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 08:25 EST, 13 November 2026

There are few sights more incendiary to the modern manager than a footballer reaching for his phone as soon as he walks through the dressing room door. So you can imagine the reaction Jake O’Brien received when he pulled out his mobile just before one half-time team talk.

But the Everton and Republic of Ireland defender had a good excuse: he’s the only Type One diabetic playing in the Premier League.

O’Brien’s body is unable to create insulin, the hormone that regulates the amount of glucose in your blood.

Loaded on his mobile is an app linked via Bluetooth to a circular device on his arm which gives a reading of his blood sugar levels. It is then that he takes out a needle and injects the necessary insulin dose into his thigh or stomach.

‘There was one guy who didn’t react too well. Mentioning no names! He was saying: "What are you doing on your phone?"' O’Brien recalls. ‘But he soon realised what it was for.’

It can also come as a shock to the uninitiated among his team-mates.

‘One or two are taken aback at first,’ he says. ‘It can be a bit confusing. “What’s he doing?’’ Or maybe those that are a little squeamish, but they soon get used to it. It's only a small needle.'

Everton and Ireland defender Jake O'Brien is the only diabetic footballer in the Premier League

O'Brien (pictured attending an awareness workshop put on by Everton) revels in the role of being a diabetes ambassador

O'Brien (pictured with his partner Sophie) says some of his team-mates are 'taken aback' when he injects himself with insulin (Source: Instagram/Obrienjake_)

Tracking blood glucose levels is now an everyday part of O'Brien's life but it is a life that was unwittingly put in jeopardy prior to his diagnosis at 16.

O’Brien was later told he had been just one day away from slipping into a coma when his concerned parents ushered him to the doctors near the family home in Youghal, County Cork, for a check-up.

Their sports-mad son, who had won national titles at boxing and hurling, was tired, losing weight and had an insatiable thirst despite drinking eight to nine litres of water a day. He had lost seven kilograms in just over a week. A blood test revealed his blood sugar was ten times what was considered stable and he was rushed to hospital.

‘I was told I was a day away from a coma,' says O'Brien. 'If I had gone to sleep that night without having gone to the doctor, who knows?’

He went into hospital that night weighing 53kg, or just over eight stone. Two weeks post-diagnosis he was back up to 60kg, and within two years he had put on a whopping 30kg.

'Yeah, 30kg,' laughs O'Brien. 'I know it's not normal. It must have been some grocery bill for Mum, but I was motivated to put on the weight, going to the gym all the time.

‘I was a bit naive about it all,' he deadpans. ‘I never expected to have anything but once I knew what diabetes was, I didn’t wallow in it, I took it as a positive. Everything just clicked for me physically. I just thought, "Right, now I know what’s wrong, I can get on with my life again".

‘It was a pain going in and out of hospital, but I just took it as education and wanted to get my sport back on track.

'My family are... I wouldn't say cold, but matter of fact. Supportive, obviously, but they are all sporty too, so it was just, "Get on with it".'

O'Brien's life in the Premier League would have seemed inconceivable when he fell down to 53kg as a teenager and was hospitalised

He is now an imposing 6ft 6in tall, weighing around 96kg. His physique offers no outward indication of the daily challenge he is dealing with

Today, relaxing in the cafe at Everton’s Finch Farm training complex, O’Brien is an imposing 6ft 6in tall, weighing around 96kg. His physique offers no outward indication of the daily challenge he is dealing with.

There’s a Cork-lilt to his softly spoken Irish tone. He’s polite and engaging and it’s clear he revels in the role of being a diabetes ambassador, spreading the message that diagnosis doesn’t have to end your dreams.

Such has been his impact, he has even attracted support from fans of the other club in the city.

One, six-year-old Liverpool fan Louis, reached out via Instagram to ask O’Brien how he kept up his glucose levels during a game and whether he suffered any ‘hypos’ - the expression for hypoglycemic episodes, when the blood sugar drops too low and leaves you faint or dizzy.

Louis, whose siblings Paisley and Evie also have Type One diabetes, followed up by challenging O’Brien to a penalty shootout. If the Everton man lost, he faced a forfeit, he would have to shout ‘Up the Reds’ on social media.

‘You play for the wrong team but you're still a Type One hero, and Mum says you're proof that diabetes doesn't stop you from playing at the top level,’ posted Louis.

Touched by the message, O’Brien asked Everton to invite the youngster and his family to training for a kickabout, although ultimately, we are assured they reached a compromise on the penalties forfeit.

‘I’ve struck up a rapport with some kids and groups here and in Ireland,' says O'Brien. 'They often have the same story as mine of not being sure what the future holds.

‘There’s a big misconception about diabetes over what it is and the limitations it brings.

‘Just because you have diabetes doesn’t mean your dreams are over.’

‘Adrenaline is higher on match days so that can change how you feel. I may inject four times before a night game and a bit more at half-time'

‘Just because you have diabetes doesn’t mean your dreams are over,’ says O'Brien, who also excelled at boxing and hurling as a boy (Source: TikTok/Everton)

The centre back credits boxing for helping discipline with his diet but underlines ‘no food is off limits, it’s just about applying common sense'.

A typical day sees him eat eggs, salmon and dates for breakfast to match his insulin doses to the carbohydrates he’s taking on around 9.30am before training. Afterwards he’ll have a light lunch at 2pm then take something back from the training ground for a light evening meal.

‘I just have to watch carbohydrates. I’ll eat more of them on match day but then work out my insulin ratio to the amount I eat and whether I need to inject more.

‘Adrenaline is higher on match days so that can change how you feel, I may inject four times before a night game and inject a bit more at half-time. If it’s not quite right you may get a bit heavy-legged or if I get a few cramps I may need a gel. But I've had no dangerous episodes.'

When World Diabetes Day dawns on Saturday, O’Brien will be fully focused on preparing to play for Ireland in Austria in the Nations League.

It will give him a chance to revert to his favoured centre back position having been asked to fill in predominantly at right back under David Moyes.

He acknowledges it's not his preferred role but dismisses rumours that he wanted to leave as a result in the summer.

'There was nothing in that,' O'Brien affirms. ‘I was never close to leaving.

'People know I'm not a natural right back but I'll play wherever I need to, to help the team. We're only a small squad so it’s important everyone chips in.

‘There’s a lot of different right backs. I see Arsenal have centre backs playing at right back so I can take pointers from them but then again, I am 6ft 6in so I’m not the average shape.’

O'Brien insists there was 'nothing in' reports that he wanted to leave Everton last summer to get more minutes at his preferred position of centre back

At least O’Brien has former Everton captain Seamus Coleman on hand for advice.

‘Seamus is a good friend. He still gives me pointers of where to be, positioning wise and seeing the game differently.'

Ireland assistant John O'Shea, a versatile defender himself in his Manchester United days, is another mentor. O’Shea and Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrímsson were at Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch O'Brien play his part in Everton's recent Carabao Cup win over Newcastle.

'Heimir is a good guy,' says O'Brien. 'Very understanding. It's always a nice change of scenery to link up with Ireland. We've got a difficult couple of games (Austria and Kosovo) but hopefully if we get two wins it’s within reach.'

Indeed, if there's a mantra that personifies O'Brien's outlook on life, no matter what knocks you take, it is: always believe you can still achieve.

'Don’t be afraid and don’t let anything hold you back, that's what I say.'
